title: mode-A answer batch output (NNN.out.json)
description: The contract between the answering agent (`brain-analyst` in mode A, which is handed the retrieved context and NO tools) and `brain eval answers merge`. Mode A measures retrieval, not the agent: the only admissible source for an answer is the `context[]` of its own case, so every claim must be traceable to an item that was handed to you. Merge applies this file in two halves. The ENVELOPE (`batch_id`, `answers` being an array, no unknown top-level field) decides whether the batch is readable at all; a batch that fails it goes to `retry/` and, after two more attempts, to `quarantine/`. Everything under `$defs` is checked per answer: one bad answer is rejected and counted, the rest of the batch merges. Two rules merge adds that a schema cannot state: `case_id` must be a case of the matching `.in.json`, and every entry of `cited_keys` must be a key or chunk id that appears in THAT case's context — a citation that is not is kept with the answer and marked invalid, because a citation habit that invents keys is a measurement, not a parse error.

batch_id.description: Exactly the `batch_id` of the .in.json this answers, e.g. "shard-02/004".

answers.description: One entry per case in the input, in any order. A case you cannot answer is still an entry — with the refusal as its `answer` and `confidence: "none"` — never a silently missing one. A case left out is reported as unanswered against the strategy that retrieved its context, which would read as that strategy's failure.

notes.description: Free-text remarks for the planner — a context whose items contradict each other, a question whose language is ambiguous. Never a place to hide a rule you could not follow: that is a `failed` entry in status.json.

case_id.description: The `case_id` of the case you are answering, copied exactly from the input (`<question id>.<label>`). Not a case of this batch = the answer is rejected and counted.

answer.description: The answer, in the LANGUAGE OF THE QUESTION (`lang` in the case), written only from that case's `context[]`. Every factual sentence ends with citations in square brackets: `[KAFKA-14649]`, `[KIP-848]`, `[XT-10007]`, `[chunk:ab12cd34…]` (at least 8 hex characters), `[a1b2c3d4]` for a commit, `[person:jira:mjsax]`, `[community:L0-6]`. A key in running prose is not a citation — only the brackets count. When the context does not hold the answer, say so plainly ("not in context" / "לא נמצא בהקשר") and stop; do not fill the gap from prior knowledge about Kafka, and do not answer a different question than the one asked.

cited_keys.description: Every key or chunk id you cited in `answer`, once each, spelled exactly as the context spells it (a chunk id may be given in full or as the prefix you cited). This is the machine-readable copy of your brackets: merge checks it against the context you were given and against the graph, and a mismatch between this list and the brackets in your text is itself reported.

confidence.description: How well the context supported the answer. `high` = every claim rests on an item you cited. `medium` = the context answers the question partly, or you had to read across items. `low` = the context only touches the subject and you are reporting what little it says. `none` = the context does not answer the question at all; the `answer` then says exactly that. Never a measure of how confident you feel about Kafka — only about this context.

unanswerable_reason.description: Only with `confidence: "none"`: one sentence naming what the context is missing ("no item names a test that covers KAFKA-14649"). It is read as evidence about the retrieval, so name the gap, not your uncertainty.
